gaps.sentence: He took ___ notice of the warning and carried on as before.
gaps.explanation: 'Take little notice of' means to pay hardly any attention; 'notice' is uncountable here.

gaps.sentence: The twins are ___ over six feet tall.
gaps.explanation: 'Both' is used for exactly two; 'all' is for three or more.

gaps.sentence: If you walk instead of driving, you'll spend ___ on petrol.
gaps.explanation: 'Spend less' is the comparative with uncountable money; 'fewer' is for countable nouns.

gaps.sentence: He had ___ money, so he couldn't even buy a bus ticket.
gaps.explanation: 'Had no money' states zero and explains the result; 'none' cannot stand directly before a noun.

gaps.hint: general statement without 'the' — 'people' has no article
gaps.explanation: 'Most people' means people in general; 'most of' needs 'the' (most of the people).

gaps.sentence: It took a great ___ of courage to admit the mistake.
gaps.explanation: 'A great deal of courage' is the standard pattern with uncountables; 'a great number of' needs countables.

gaps.sentence: It's so quiet here — there's hardly ___ around.
gaps.explanation: 'Hardly' is a negative adverb, so it combines with 'anybody' (hardly anybody = almost nobody); 'nobody' would double the negative.

gaps.sentence: ___ of work has been done on the house since we bought it.
gaps.explanation: 'A lot of work' fits the pattern '___ of work'; 'much of work' would need 'the', and 'few' is for countables.
